title: Galaxies: islands of stars
subtitle: Our own galaxy seen from the inside, the shapes of others, and which ones you can really see.

sections.heading: The galaxy we live in
body: After this lesson you will be able to explain what the Milky Way is, find the one galaxy visible to the naked eye from the north, and name the main galaxy shapes.

A galaxy is an enormous system of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. Ours, the Milky Way, holds a few hundred billion stars arranged mostly in a thin disc roughly 100,000 light-years across, with a central bulge. The Sun sits in the disc about 26,000 light-years from the center. Every star you can see with the naked eye belongs to the Milky Way.

Because we are inside the disc, we see it edge-on, as a hazy band of light circling the whole sky: the combined glow of stars too distant to separate. The band is brightest and widest toward Sagittarius, because that is the direction of the galaxy's center. City lights erase the band completely; under a dark sky it is one of the great sights of nature.

steps.caption: A dark August sky from mid-northern latitudes. The Milky Way runs from Cygnus overhead down to Sagittarius in the south. You are looking along the disc of our own galaxy.

The same August evening from mid-southern latitudes (34°S): the brightest part of the band, around Sagittarius and Scorpius, passes almost overhead. The southern hemisphere has the finest view of the galaxy's center.

The center of the galaxy lies just off the spout of the Sagittarius Teapot, 26,000 light-years away and hidden behind dust. Slide the light-pollution control toward 9 to see what a big city does to the band.

figures.caption: We live inside a thin disc, about halfway out. Aim your line of sight along the disc and it passes through tens of thousands of light-years of stars: that is the band. Tilt it out of the disc and you are into dark intergalactic space after a few hundred light-years.

image.alt: A panorama of the whole sky with the Milky Way as a bright band running straight across the middle, brightest and dustiest at the centre
image.kindNote: 360-degree mosaic of photographs of the whole sky, arranged so the Milky Way runs across the middle

figures.caption: The whole sky in one picture, arranged so that the disc of our galaxy runs across the middle. The band is the disc seen edge-on from inside; the bright bulge at the centre lies towards Sagittarius, crossed by dark lanes of dust. The two smudges below right are the Magellanic Clouds.

misconception.myth: Pictures of the Milky Way’s spiral arms are photographs taken from outside it.
misconception.fact: No spacecraft has ever left the Milky Way, or come anywhere close. Every face-on picture of our galaxy is an illustration, built from measurements of where stars and gas lie. The only real photographs of the Milky Way are taken from inside, and they show the band.

sections.heading: Other galaxies and their shapes
body: In the 1920s Edwin Hubble showed that many of the faint "spiral nebulae" are separate galaxies far outside our own, and sorted them by shape. Spiral galaxies are flat discs with winding arms where new stars form: [[dso:M31|the Andromeda Galaxy]], [[dso:M51|the Whirlpool]] and [[dso:M81|M81]]. In barred spirals the arms start from the ends of a straight bar of stars across the center: [[dso:M83|M83]] in Hydra and NGC 1365 in Fornax are fine examples, and the Milky Way itself is a barred spiral.

Elliptical galaxies are smooth balls or ovals of mostly old stars with little gas and no arms; the giants [[dso:M87|M87]] and [[dso:M49|M49]] in Virgo are of this kind. Lenticular galaxies are in between: a disc and bulge but no spiral arms. Irregular galaxies have no tidy shape at all, such as the two Magellanic Clouds, small companions of the Milky Way visible to the naked eye from the southern hemisphere, and [[dso:M82|M82]], a galaxy churned up by a burst of star formation.

check.prompt: What kind of galaxy is the Milky Way?
choices: A barred spiral
An elliptical
An irregular
A lenticular
check.explanation: The Milky Way is a disc galaxy with spiral arms that start from a bar of stars across its centre: a barred spiral.

sections.heading: Looking back in time
body: Galaxy distances are measured in millions of light-years. Light from the Andromeda Galaxy has traveled about 2.5 million years to reach you: you see it as it was before our species existed. The Virgo galaxies are more than 50 million light-years away. To look far into space is always to look into the past.

Galaxies gather in groups and clusters. The Milky Way and Andromeda are the two heavyweights of the Local Group, a family of several dozen galaxies, most of them small, that also includes the spiral [[dso:M33|M33]] in Triangulum. The nearest big cluster, the Virgo Cluster, holds well over a thousand galaxies.

figures.caption: The farther away something is, the older the light you see. Sunlight is 8 minutes old; the Andromeda Galaxy’s light set out 2.5 million years ago, before our species existed. Slide out to the earliest galaxies and you are looking back almost to the beginning.

thinkAbout.question: Suppose astronomers in the Andromeda Galaxy have a telescope powerful enough to see the surface of the Earth. What would they see today?
thinkAbout.answer: The Earth as it was about 2.5 million years ago, because the light reaching them now left Earth back then: no cities, no farms, no modern humans, only early human relatives in Africa. Looking across space always means looking into the past, in both directions.

sections.heading: The realm of galaxies
body: Seen from mid-northern latitudes on March–May evenings, the Milky Way band lies low around the horizon and we look straight up out of the disc, away from its dust. That window, between the tail of Leo and the stars of Virgo and Coma Berenices, is crowded with galaxies; observers call it the realm of galaxies. The heart of the Virgo Cluster lies about halfway between [[star:Denebola|Denebola]] and [[star:Vindemiatrix|Vindemiatrix]]. From the southern hemisphere the same window is up in the north on April–June evenings, lower but still well placed.

steps.caption: An April evening. The markers crowding the gap between Denebola (Leo's tail) and Vindemiatrix (in Virgo) are galaxies of the Virgo Cluster, over 50 million light-years away.

figures.caption: Looking straight out of the disc, your line of sight leaves the galaxy after only a few hundred light-years, so little dust or starlight gets in the way. That clear window, towards Virgo and Coma Berenices, is why one part of the spring sky in the northern hemisphere is crowded with galaxies.

thinkAbout.question: Very few galaxies are found in the parts of the sky close to the Milky Way band. Is that because there are fewer galaxies in those directions?
thinkAbout.answer: No. Galaxies are spread fairly evenly in every direction, but when we look along the disc of our own galaxy its dust clouds block the light from beyond. Astronomers call this strip the zone of avoidance; infrared and radio telescopes, which see through dust, find plenty of galaxies there.

sections.heading: What you can actually see
body: Galaxies are the hardest common targets, because their light is spread thin and city skyglow swamps it. One is within reach of the naked eye from the north: [[dso:M31|the Andromeda Galaxy]], a faint elongated smudge under a dark sky and a binocular object from the suburbs. From a big city, binoculars may just show its bright core on a clear moonless night. From mid-southern latitudes Andromeda stays low in the north, and the two Magellanic Clouds are the naked-eye galaxies instead. Everything else wants a telescope and, above all, a dark sky, and even then you see a soft gray glow, not the spiral arms of the photographs.

To find Andromeda, start at [[star:Alpheratz|Alpheratz]], the corner star of the Great Square of Pegasus. Hop two stars along Andromeda's chain to [[star:Mirach|Mirach]], turn a right angle, and go past the fainter star [[star:μ And|Mu Andromedae]] the same distance again.

steps.caption: From the corner of the Great Square, follow the chain to Mirach, turn right, and step past Mu Andromedae to the galaxy. Its light left 2.5 million years ago.

images.alt: The Andromeda Galaxy photographed with a 130 mm amateur telescope: a long oval glow with a bright core and dark dust lanes

check.prompt: You find the Andromeda Galaxy in binoculars. What are you most likely to see?
choices: A small, soft grey oval with a brighter centre
A spiral with blue arms
Thousands of separate stars
A bright point like a planet
check.explanation: Its light is spread thin and it is millions of light-years away, so by eye and in binoculars it is a faint grey oval glow, brightest at the core.

sections.tryIt: On a moonless October–December evening (it is low in the north from the southern hemisphere), get away from direct lights, let your eyes adapt for ten minutes, and sweep binoculars from Mirach past Mu Andromedae. A small gray oval that will not focus to a point is another galaxy.

keyPoints: The Milky Way band is our own galaxy's disc seen from inside; its center is toward Sagittarius.
Galaxies come as spirals, barred spirals, ellipticals, lenticulars and irregulars.
Galaxies are millions of light-years away, so we see them as they were millions of years ago.
From the northern hemisphere, March–May evenings face out of the Milky Way's disc toward the Virgo Cluster, the realm of galaxies.
Only the Andromeda Galaxy is a naked-eye galaxy from mid-northern latitudes; from the southern hemisphere the Magellanic Clouds are too. Most galaxies need a telescope and a dark sky.

examples.label: Andromeda Galaxy (M31)
examples.note: Large spiral 2.5 million light-years away. Naked eye from a dark site; binoculars elsewhere.

examples.label: Triangulum Galaxy (M33)
examples.note: Face-on spiral, third-largest member of the Local Group. Binoculars under a truly dark sky; its glow is very spread out.

examples.label: M81
examples.note: Bright spiral near the Big Dipper. A small oval glow in binoculars from a dark site or in a small telescope.

examples.label: M82
examples.note: Irregular starburst galaxy beside M81. A thin gray streak in a small telescope.

examples.label: Whirlpool Galaxy (M51)
examples.note: Face-on spiral with a small companion. Two fuzzy spots in a small telescope under a dark sky; arms need a larger one.

examples.label: M87
examples.note: Giant elliptical at the heart of the Virgo Cluster. A round featureless glow in a small telescope under a dark sky.

examples.label: M83
examples.note: Barred spiral in Hydra. Low in the south from mid-northern latitudes, high from the southern hemisphere; a small telescope and a dark sky are needed.

questions.prompt: Why does the Milky Way appear as a band across the sky instead of a spiral?
choices: It is a ring-shaped galaxy
We are inside its flat disc and see the disc edge-on all around us
Only one spiral arm is lit up at a time
The Earth's atmosphere stretches its light into a band
questions.explanation: From inside a thin disc of stars, the disc wraps around you as a band. You would have to leave the galaxy to see its spiral shape.

questions.prompt: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away. What does that mean for what you see?
choices: You see it as it is at this moment
You see it as it will be in 2.5 million years
Its light takes 2.5 million seconds to arrive
You see light that left it about 2.5 million years ago
questions.explanation: A light-year is the distance light covers in a year, so the light arriving tonight set out about 2.5 million years ago.

questions.prompt: A galaxy is a smooth oval glow of old stars with no disc, arms or obvious gas clouds. What type is it?
choices: Elliptical
Spiral
Barred spiral
Irregular
questions.explanation: Ellipticals such as M87 are smooth and armless. Spirals have discs with arms; irregulars have no regular shape.

questions.prompt: Why is spring the best season for hunting galaxies from the northern hemisphere?
choices: Galaxies are closer to us in spring
Spring nights are the longest
In the evening we face out of the Milky Way's dusty disc, toward the Virgo Cluster
The Moon is absent in spring
questions.explanation: The disc's dust hides galaxies behind the Milky Way band. In spring the band is low and we look out through the clear 'window' toward Virgo and Coma.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a realistic expectation for a galaxy in a small telescope?
choices: Colorful spiral arms like the photographs
A soft gray glow, brighter toward the middle
Individual stars filling the eyepiece
Nothing; galaxies can only be photographed
questions.explanation: Galaxies are faint and spread out. Visually they are gray glows; arms and color come from long-exposure photographs.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Local Group is correct?
choices: It is another name for the solar system
It is the cluster of galaxies in Virgo
It contains only the Milky Way
It is our small family of galaxies, dominated by the Milky Way and Andromeda
questions.explanation: The Local Group has several dozen members, mostly dwarfs, with the Milky Way and the Andromeda Galaxy as its two large spirals.
